title: Containerization Deep Dive
summary: A container is not a tiny computer — it's one ordinary Linux process wearing blinders and a leash. Namespaces decide what it sees; cgroups decide what it gets.

blocks.markdown:
A container is just a normal process on the host's kernel — there is no second OS inside it.

- Two old kernel features make it feel isolated: **namespaces** (what it can *see*) and **cgroups** (what it can *use*).
- A **container image** is a stack of read-only layers; the running container adds one thin writable layer on top.
- **Docker** wraps these primitives in a friendly workflow; **OCI** standardizes the format so any runtime can run any image.
- The "oh, that's all it is" feeling is correct — no magic VM, no embedded OS, no emulation.

blocks.subTitle: Why it exists
blocks.markdown:
Containers give VM-like isolation and reproducibility without a duplicated OS per instance.

- **"Works on my machine"** — ship code *plus* its exact dependencies as one frozen, layered artifact.
- **VM waste** — a full guest OS costs GBs of disk, hundreds of MB idle RAM, and 10–60s to boot. Fifty services means fifty duplicated kernels.
- **The insight** — Linux already isolated most of that via chroot, cgroups, and namespaces. Docker just made them usable.

blocks.subTitle: Namespaces — what it can see
blocks.markdown:
A namespace gives a process its own private instance of a global resource.

- **PID** — its first process is PID 1; `ps` shows only the container's own processes.
- **Mount** — its own root `/`, which is how the image becomes the filesystem.
- **Network** — its own interfaces and ports, so two containers can both bind 8080.
- **UTS / User / IPC** — own hostname, own UID mapping (root inside ≠ root outside), own shared memory.

Entered via `clone()`/`unshare()` with `CLONE_NEW*` flags. Nothing is copied — the kernel just keeps separate tables.

blocks.subTitle: cgroups — what it can use
blocks.markdown:
Control groups cap how much a group of processes can consume.

![Namespaces and cgroups combining into a container](assets/containerization-deep/namespaces-cgroups.svg)

- **cpu** — CPU time / shares.
- **memory** — a hard ceiling; exceed it and the kernel OOM-kills a process in the group.
- **io** — disk bandwidth; **pids** — max processes, to stop fork bombs.
- `docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5` just writes these numbers into the container's cgroup.

Namespaces give a private *view*; cgroups give a metered *budget*. Together, that's a container.

blocks.subTitle: Images & layers
blocks.markdown:
An image is a stack of read-only layers merged by a union filesystem.

![Container image as stacked union-fs layers](assets/containerization-deep/image-layers.svg)

- Each Dockerfile step (`FROM`, `RUN`, `COPY`) records one layer of filesystem *changes*.
- A union FS (OverlayFS) merges them, then adds one thin **writable layer** on top.
- Writes use **copy-on-write**: the file is copied up before being modified, leaving read-only layers intact.
- Each layer is content-addressed by SHA-256, so a shared base layer is stored and shipped once.

assets.alt: Container image as stacked union-fs layers

blocks.subTitle: Docker, containerd, runc
blocks.markdown:
Docker is a client/server toolkit that delegates the kernel-touching work downward.

- The **CLI** sends commands to the **daemon** (`dockerd`) over a socket.
- `dockerd` builds images and wires networking, then hands lifecycle to **containerd**, which calls **runc** — the small OCI runtime that makes the namespace/cgroup syscalls and starts the process.
- **Registries** (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR) store content-addressed layers; `push`/`pull` move only the layers you don't already have.

The point: keep the friendly tooling separate from the minimal, auditable thing that touches the kernel.

blocks.subTitle: The Dockerfile cache
blocks.markdown:
Order steps least-to-most changing so expensive layers stay cached.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim        # shared base, ~150 MB
COPY requirements.txt .       # deps manifest
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  # slow, ~40 MB
COPY . .                      # your code, ~2 MB, changes often
CMD ["python", "server.py"]
```

- Change one line of code and only the last `COPY` layer rebuilds — deps stay cached.
- `push` then ships just the ~2 MB code layer; teammates pull only what they're missing.
- Put slow, rarely-changing steps *below* fast, frequently-changing ones.

blocks.subTitle: Containers vs VMs
blocks.markdown:
Containers share one kernel; VMs each carry a full guest OS on a hypervisor.

![Container stack vs VM stack](assets/containerization-deep/container-vs-vm.svg)

| Aspect | Containers | VMs |
|---|---|---|
| Kernel | Shared host | Own per VM |
| Boot | 50–200 ms | 10–60 s |
| Isolation | Weaker | Hardware-level |

That single duplicated guest-OS box is the entire weight, boot-time, and isolation difference.

blocks.subTitle: Picking the boundary
blocks.markdown:
Trade isolation strength against density and speed.

- **Untrusted / multi-tenant code** → VMs or sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata, Firecracker microVMs).
- **Different kernel or kernel modules** → you *must* use a VM; containers can't change the kernel.
- **Fast deploys, high density of trusted services** → plain containers.
- **Pulled often or run everywhere** → invest in shrinking the image (slim, distroless); built rarely → don't over-optimize.
- Always set **memory limits** in production to contain leaks ([cloud-kubernetes](cloud-kubernetes)).

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
The same primitives run the platforms you deploy on.

- **Kubernetes** talks to any OCI runtime via the **CRI**, so "K8s deprecates Docker" never touched your images — only the node shim changed.
- **OCI** standardizes the image, runtime, and registry specs, so a Docker-built image runs under Podman or CRI-O unchanged.
- **AWS Firecracker** — a microVM booting its own kernel in ~125 ms; VM-grade isolation at near-container speed for Lambda/Fargate.
- **Google gVisor** — a user-space kernel intercepting syscalls to shrink the attack surface for untrusted code.

blocks.subTitle: Limits firing & signals
blocks.markdown:
A limit firing looks different depending on which limit it is.

- **Exit code 137** = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL) — almost always the kernel OOM killer hitting `memory.max`. Check the limit and actual usage.
- A **CPU limit throttles** (runs slower); a **memory limit is hard** (kills you). Watch `cpu.stat` throttled periods for hidden latency.
- **Crash loops** with code 137 or 1 signal OOM, bad config, or a failing dependency.
- **Persistent data must live in a volume** — the writable layer dies with the container.

The misconceptions that bite in interviews and on-call:

- **"A container is a lightweight VM."** No guest OS inside — it's a host process with a restricted view. This explains both the speed and the weaker isolation.
- **"Containers are secure by default."** Shared kernel; `--privileged`, running as root, or mounting `docker.sock` hands over the host.
- **"Data in a container persists."** The writable layer dies with it — use a volume.
- **"Set high limits to be safe."** No memory limit lets a leak take down the whole node; set from measurements.
- **"One process per container is optional."** PID 1 has special signal/zombie duties — use a real init like `tini` if you must run several.
